blocks.content: Have you ever written a block ofif-elsestatements just to decide which object to create?
It works. Until you add more types. Until the same block appears in five places. Until every new type means editing existing code.
This is exactly what the Factory Method Pattern fixes.
Instead of scattering new keywords everywhere, the Factory Method gives you one clean place to create objects without hardwiring your code to specific classes.
It is useful when:
["The exact type needed is not known until runtime.","Object creation logic is complex or repetitive.","You want new types without touching existing code."]
items: The exact type needed is not known until runtime.
Object creation logic is complex or repetitive.
You want new types without touching existing code.

blocks.content: Let's walk through a real example and see how it works.
1. The Problem: Processing Payments
Imagine you are building an e-commerce app that processes payments. At first, it is simple. You only support credit card payments.
A single class takes care of that.
To use it in our service, we create the payment object and call theprocess()method.
All good. But then comes a new requirement: support PayPal payments.
So you add a new class and update PaymentService with a new if block.
Slightly more complex but still manageable. Then the business wants crypto payments. Then bank transfers. Then Apple Pay.
Each one adds another branch:
Now, PaymentService has become a giant control tower. It creates every type of payment, knows how each one works, and decides which one to use all in a single place.
Here’s what the dependency structure looks like:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784838129884-536829892.png
blocks.alt: The problem - PaymentService depends on every payment type

blocks.content: Adding a sixth payment method means modifying PaymentService yet again.
This becomes a nightmare to maintain:

["Every new payment method forces you to modify the same core class.","Testing is painful because object creation is tangled with business logic.","It violates the Open/Closed Principle the class cannot be extended without modification."]
items: Every new payment method forces you to modify the same core class.
Testing is painful because object creation is tangled with business logic.
It violates the Open/Closed Principle the class cannot be extended without modification.

blocks.content: 2. Simple Factory: A First Attempt
Before jumping to the full Factory Method pattern, there is a common intermediate step: extract the creation logic into a separate class.
This is called the Simple Factory. It is not a formal Gang of Four pattern, but it is one of the most practical refactoring techniques in real-world codebases.

The idea is straightforward: create a separate class whose only job is to centralize object creation. The payment service no longer needs to know which concrete class to instantiate. It asks the factory.
All creation logic is now in one place.PaymentServiceis now much cleaner:
This is much better. The service only uses the payment object it does not construct it.
Adding new types becomes easier because you only modify the factory, not every service that depends on payments.

But as your product grows and you continue adding new payment methods, something starts to feel off again. Your SimplePaymentFactory is beginning to look eerily similar to the bloated code you just refactored away from.
Every time you introduce a new payment method cryptocurrency, BNPL, gift cards you’re right back to modifying the same switch statement.
That’s not very Open/Closed, is it?
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784838130285-397853065.png
blocks.alt: Simple Factory - centralized creation, must edit for new types

blocks.content: Your system is better but it is still not open to extension without modification. You are still hardcoding the decision logic and centralizing creation in one place. Every new payment method means reopening this class and editing it.
You need each payment type to take responsibility for its own creation instead of one factory knowing about all of them.
And that is exactly the problem the Factory Method Pattern was designed to solve.
3. What is the Factory Method Pattern?
blocks.text: 3. What is the Factory Method Pattern?

blocks.content: The Factory Method Pattern takes object creation and hands it off to subclasses. Instead of one central factory deciding what to create, you delegate that responsibility to specialized classes that each know exactly what they need to produce.
In simpler terms:

["Each subclass defines its own way of creating an object.","The base class defines a common interface for creation but never decides what the object actually is.","The base class defines the workflow subclasses fill in the details."]
items: Each subclass defines its own way of creating an object.
The base class defines a common interface for creation but never decides what the object actually is.
The base class defines the workflow subclasses fill in the details.

Real-World Analogy
Think of a car manufacturing company.
If the system works like a Simple Factory, there is one central factory floor that decides whether to build a sedan, an SUV, or a truck. All construction logic lives in that single place.
With the Factory Method, things are organized differently. Each specialized plant the Sedan Plant, the SUV Plant, the Truck Plant knows exactly how to build its own vehicle.
The company headquarters doesn’t worry about how each vehicle is built. It simply tells the appropriate plant to start production.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784837815182-717880169.png
blocks.alt: Factory Method pattern - UML class diagram

blocks.content: The Four Participants
The Factory Method pattern is built around four core roles. Each one has a clear responsibility, and together they decouple object creation from object usage.
1. Product Payment

The interface that defines the contract for all payment objects. Every concrete payment implements process(). The rest of the system only ever talks to this interface never to CreditCardPayment or PayPalPayment directly.
2. ConcreteProduct CreditCardPayment, PayPalPayment, CryptoPayment

The actual classes that implement the Paymentinterface. Each one handles its own processing logic internally. They all share the same process() signature but do completely different things behind the scenes.
3. Creator PaymentCreator

An abstract class that declares the factory method createPayment() which subclasses must implement. It also contains shared logic the processPayment() method calls createPayment() to get the right payment object and then uses it. The Creator defines the workflow. Subclasses fill in the details.
4. ConcreteCreator CreditCardPaymentCreator, PayPalPaymentCreator
Subclasses of PaymentCreator that override the factory method to return their specific payment type. Each creator is paired with exactly one product.
["CreditCardPaymentCreator returns new CreditCardPayment()","PayPalPaymentCreator returns new PayPalPayment()"]
<font face="monospace" size="4"></font>
4. How It Works
Here is the Factory Method workflow step by step:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784837815679-386819389.png

Step 1: Client selects a Creator The client decides which ConcreteCreator to use based on configuration or business logic. If the user pays by credit card, the client instantiates CreditCardPaymentCreator.
Step 2: Client calls a method on the Creator The client calls processPayment("$100"). This method lives in the abstract PaymentCreator class not in the concrete subclass.
Step 3: Creator calls the factory method Inside processPayment(), the Creator calls createPayment(). Since the Creator is abstract, this call is dispatched to the ConcreteCreator's override.

Step 4: ConcreteCreator returns a ConcreteProduct CreditCardPaymentCreator.createPayment() returns a new CreditCardPayment(). The Creator receives it as the Payment interface type it never knows the concrete class.
Step 5: Creator uses the product The Creator calls payment.process("$100") on the object it just received. The correct concrete payment behavior executes.

5. Implementing Factory Method
Let's implement the Factory Method pattern for our payment system step by step.
Step 1: Define the Product Interface
This is the contract that all payment types must follow. Any code that works with payments only depends on this interface.
Step 2: Define Concrete Products
Each payment type implements the interface with its own behavior.
Step 3: Define an Abstract Creator
We create an abstract class that declares the factory method createPayment() and includes shared behavior like processPayment() that defines the high-level logic.
The Creator defines the flow. Subclasses fill in the details.
This class does not know what payment it is processing but it knows how to process it. It defers the choice of payment type entirely to its subclasses.
Step 4: Define Concrete Creators
Each concrete creator extends the abstract creator and overrides the factory method to return its specific product.
No conditionals. No switch statements. Each class knows exactly what it creates and nothing else.

blocks.content: 6. Practical Example: Food Order System
Let's build a complete example in a different domain. We will create a food ordering system that prepares meals from different cuisines Italian, Chinese, and Mexican.
Problem
A food delivery app needs to prepare meals from different restaurant types. Each cuisine has its own preparation style, ingredients, and plating. New cuisines may be added in the future.
Step 1: Define the Product Interface
The contract every meal must follow. All client code works through this interface only.
Step 2: Define Concrete Products
Each cuisine implements the interface with its own preparation logic.
Step 3: Define the Abstract Creator
Declares the factory method and contains shared order logic. The Creator defines the workflow subclasses fill in the product.
Step 4: Define Concrete Creators
Each restaurant extends the abstract creator and returns its specific meal type.
Step 5: Client Code
Step 6: Adding a New Cuisine
Want to add Japanese food? Two new classes. Zero existing code touched.
